results.title: Valve and Collabora Announce Official Arch Linux ARM64 Port for Steam Frame - 9to5Linux
results.content:
Steam Frame uses an ARM64 processor, so Collabora, in collaboration with Valve, has been developing Holo Core as a full AArch64 port of Arch Linux intended as the base for the operating system that will power the gaming VR headset. Since Arch Linux has no official ARM64 support, Collabora had to build new tooling and CI infrastructure from scratch.

But the real challenge here was to make the entire process reproducible in CI (Continuous Integration) for a rolling-release distribution like Arch Linux, which Valve already uses on the Steam Deck and Steam Machine. For now, the result is a proof of concept rather than a finished product. [...] “We have not rebuilt the entire world (all the packages available in the Arch Linux repositories). Our initial goal is to provide the set of packages required for development and image creation for the Steam Frame,” said Denis Pynkin, Senior Software Engineer at Collabora.

An early, experimental preview of Holo Core has been made available by Collabora for early adopters and developers, allowing anyone to experiment with Arch Linux on AArch64. Binary packages, sources, and a Docker container can be downloaded from the announcement page. [...] These are drawn from a snapshot of Arch Linux’s own Git package repository, adapted as needed to compile on ARM64. The next phase is to turn this into a continuously updating system that tracks Arch Linux as it evolves, ideally in collaboration with the upstream Arch Linux community’s own efforts toward ARM64 support.

For now, curious developers and those who want to run Arch Linux on AArch64 hardware can pull the container image, spin it up with Distrobox (using QEMU emulation on x86\_64 hosts if needed), and try building packages themselves using the published preview repository linked above.

results.content:
### What does the Steam Frame's stable ARM64 software stack mean for future Valve hardware?

More than just a headset milestone. SteamOS developer Pierre-Loup Griffais stated at the Frame's November 2025 announcement that the device's use of ARM processors is a first step toward other Valve devices using ARM, including future handhelds. Proton 11.0 ARM64 graduating to the stable channel means Valve has now committed to maintaining that runtime for consumer devices — permanently establishing ARM64 as a supported instruction set in the SteamOS ecosystem. Any future Steam Deck successor or ARM-based Valve portable device will run on the same software foundation the Frame is now validating. The Steam Frame is the proof-of-concept; the stable ARM64 stack is the platform. [...] Valve engineer Jeremy Selan described the design intent at the November 2025 announcement, in remarks cited by TechTimes: "One of the superpowers of SteamOS is that it decouples the games you're playing from the hardware you're running it on." The Proton 11.0 ARM64 stable promotion is that decoupling arriving at production readiness. SteamOS developer Pierre-Loup Griffais noted at the announcement, as confirmed by the Wikipedia Steam Frame article, that the Frame's ARM processor use is a first step toward other Valve devices using ARM — including future handhelds — which means the stable-channel graduation of Proton 11.0 ARM64 is not only a Frame story. It is Valve permanently committing the stable software foundation for its future ARM hardware ecosystem. [...] Native ARM64 SteamOS builds are the fastest path: the game compiles directly for the Snapdragon 8 Gen 3 and runs without translation. Windows x86 games go through Proton — which translates DirectX graphics API calls to Vulkan and handles the Windows-to-Linux operating environment transition — and then through FEX, which recompiles the x86-64 machine code to ARM64 instructions the chip can execute. FEX uses JIT compilation: the first time a code path runs, it is translated and the translation is cached; subsequent executions use the cached ARM64 version, reducing overhead over time. results.title: Valve’s SteamOS stack now covers Windows, x86 and Android on Arm | MLQ News
results.content:
## The developer workflow is explicit

Steam Frame’s development tools expose the distinction among the runtimes. Valve’s Devkit Client lets developers select Android for an APK, Steam Linux Runtime 3.0 ARM64 for a native Linux build or Steam Play for a Windows executable. Developers must enable Developer Mode, pair the headset with a host PC and upload the build through the SteamOS Devkit Client. ( [...] The route is not simply a matter of uploading any mobile package and assuming it will behave like a PC game. Valve’s engine guidance recommends Android 10 or Linux ARM64 for new Steam Frame development. Its Unity guidance specifies ARM64, recommends Vulkan or OpenGL, and calls for Steam Frame Controller support through the relevant OpenXR interaction profile. ( Those requirements make Android compatibility useful for developers with an existing mobile VR pipeline, but they do not eliminate testing for input, graphics, performance and platform services.

## The developer workflow is explicit [...] FEX addresses processor architecture. Steam Frame uses a Snapdragon 8 Gen 3 with an Arm64 instruction set, while most traditional PC games target x86 or x86-64 processors. FEX translates x86 instructions to Arm64 and forwards graphics calls to native host libraries such as Vulkan or OpenGL. Valve also cites code caching as a way to reduce stutter. (

That creates a layered path for many PC games: Proton handles Windows compatibility while FEX handles x86-to-Arm translation. A native Linux ARM64 build can avoid those translation steps, but Valve’s stated preference is to let developers maintain one well-tested version where possible rather than create a lightly supported port. results.title: Steam Frame (Steamworks Documentation)
results.content:
Steam Frame

Steamworks Documentation > Steam Hardware > Steam Frame

Steam Frame is a standalone virtual reality headset designed primarily for low-latency streaming of player's Steam Library from a PC, while also supporting standalone experiences for both VR and Non-VR. The headset integrates high-resolution displays, inside-out tracking, integrated audio, and full gamepad input into a self-contained system running SteamOS. By maintaining full compatibility with SteamVR and OpenXR, Steam Frame provides a consistent development target across streamed PC VR content and on-device applications. Supported execution models include Windows and Linux PC titles as well as native ARM64 and Android-based APKs.
